# India’s Energy Storage Boom Set to Ignite in 2026

India’s energy storage sector is entering a decisive phase. After years of policy development, tendering activity, and early‑stage deployments, 2026 is shaping up to be the year when large‑scale storage finally moves from planning to execution.

A record 224 GWh of storage capacity has been tendered to date — including 92 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) and 132 GWh of pumped hydro storage (PHS) — and projects awarded since mid‑2023 are now approaching commissioning.

At the same time, independent market analyses forecast a ten‑fold increase in installed BESS capacity, jumping from 507 MWh in 2025 to around 5 GWh in 2026. This marks a structural shift in India’s power system as the country accelerates renewable integration, grid flexibility, and peak‑shaving capabilities.

2026 will be the year India’s storage sector is tested — not on ambition, but on delivery.

## 1. From Tendering to Execution: A Historic Pipeline Takes Shape

The India Energy Storage Alliance (IESA) reports that by the end of 2025:

* 95 GWh of storage capacity is already in various stages of execution
* 80 GWh remains under tender
* 47 GWh of tenders have been cancelled
* 69 tenders totaling 102 GWh were issued in 2025 alone — nearly equal to all tenders issued between 2018 and 2024 combined

This unprecedented tendering wave reflects India’s urgent need to stabilize a grid increasingly dominated by solar and wind.

With typical development timelines of 18–24 months, the surge in 2023–2025 awards means 2026 will see the first major commissioning wave.

A key milestone will be Adani’s 1,126 MW / 3,530 MWh BESS project in Gujarat, expected to be commissioned in March 2026 — one of the largest standalone battery systems globally.

## 2. Why 2026 Is a Turning Point for India’s Storage Sector

### 2.1. Massive Capacity Additions

Multiple independent analyses confirm that India’s BESS installations will grow nearly ten‑fold in 2026, reaching 5 GWh of new capacity additions.

This growth is driven by:

* Large utility‑scale renewable projects requiring firming capacity
* Peak‑shaving and frequency regulation needs
* State‑level mandates for storage integration
* Falling global battery prices (despite short‑term volatility)

### 2.2. Commercial & Industrial (C&I) Storage Emerges

The commissioning of Juniper Green Energy’s 60 MWh merchant BESS in December 2025 marks the beginning of a new C&I‑driven storage market.

C&I customers — including data centers, manufacturing clusters, and commercial complexes — are increasingly adopting storage for:

* Peak demand management
* Backup power
* Renewable firming
* Tariff optimization

### 2.3. Policy Support Strengthens the Market

Key policy drivers include:

* Viability Gap Funding (VGF): INR 5,400 crore to support 30 GWh of standalone BESS with 20% domestic value addition requirements
* Interstate Transmission System (ISTS) charge waivers extended through 2028 for solar‑plus‑storage and pumped hydro projects
* State‑level mandates, such as Rajasthan requiring storage for renewable projects above 5 MW, and Bihar targeting 6.1 GWh of storage by 2030

These measures reduce project costs and improve bankability.

## 3. Financing Challenges and the Viability Question

Despite strong momentum, the sector faces real challenges:

### 3.1. Aggressive Tariffs Raise Concerns

Ultra‑low tariffs discovered in recent tenders have raised questions about long‑term project viability. IESA notes that only a few projects have secured financing so far, and lenders remain cautious.

### 3.2. Battery Cost Uncertainty

Global battery prices have fluctuated due to:

* Supply chain disruptions
* Trade restrictions on critical minerals
* Geopolitical tensions
* Demand surges from EV and grid‑scale markets

These uncertainties complicate financial modeling for long‑duration storage.

### 3.3. Need for Innovative Financing Structures

To unlock capital at scale, India will require:

* Hybrid revenue models (capacity + energy + ancillary services)
* Long‑term storage procurement frameworks
* Risk‑sharing mechanisms
* Green bonds and infrastructure investment trusts (InvITs)

2026 will test whether India’s storage market can attract the depth of capital required for gigawatt‑scale deployment.

## 4. Pumped Hydro Storage: The Sleeping Giant

While BESS dominates headlines, pumped hydro storage (PHS) accounts for 132 GWh of tendered capacity — more than half of India’s total storage pipeline.

PHS offers:

* Long‑duration storage
* Lower lifetime costs
* High reliability
* Grid‑scale inertia support

States like Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh are pushing multi‑GW PHS projects, positioning India as a global leader in long‑duration storage.

## 5. The Road Ahead: What Will Define Success in 2026

### 5.1. Execution at Scale

The biggest question: Can India deliver the projects it has tendered?

2026 will reveal whether aggressive bids translate into operational assets.

### 5.2. Supply Chain Localization

Domestic manufacturing of:

* Cells
* Modules
* Inverters
* EMS software
* Power conversion systems

will be critical to reducing costs and ensuring energy security.

### 5.3. Market Design Evolution

India must refine:

* Ancillary service markets
* Capacity markets
* Time‑of‑day pricing
* Storage‑specific procurement mechanisms

to ensure long‑term revenue stability.

## Conclusion: India’s Storage Sector Is Ready for Its Breakout Moment

India’s energy storage market stands at the threshold of a transformative year. With 224 GWh of tendered capacity, 5 GWh of expected BESS additions, and major projects entering commissioning, 2026 will be the year when India’s storage ambitions are tested in real‑world conditions.

If execution aligns with expectations, India will emerge as one of the world’s most dynamic storage markets — a critical foundation for achieving its renewable energy targets, strengthening grid stability, and enabling a flexible, resilient power system.

The next twelve months will determine whether India’s storage revolution becomes a global benchmark.
